hints: Look closely at cell Q - where are the dark-stained chromosomes and are they in one line in the middle or in two separate groups moving apart?
walkthrough:
Read the Chromosome Picture in Cell Q**
In cell Q you can see two distinct groups of dark chromosomes, one moving toward each end of the cell. They have already left the middle of the cell, so this is not metaphase where chromosomes line up on the equator.

Link to Anaphase**
Separation of sister chromatids to opposite poles pulled by shortening spindle fibres is the defining event of anaphase. That is exactly what cell Q shows.

hints: Think about why a healthy plant needs to keep making new genetically identical cells throughout its life, from a seedling to a large plant.
Think of two different needs: one to get bigger and one to cope with cells that become old, damaged or worn out.
walkthrough:
Why Mitosis Matters - Identical Copies**
Mitosis produces two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent. A plant uses this to increase cell number without changing the genetic information.

Two Main Jobs in a Plant**
First, for growth, for example cell division in meristems to make roots longer and shoots taller. Second, for repair and replacement, where old, dead, damaged or worn out cells are replaced to keep tissues healthy. Asexual reproduction to make genetically identical offspring is another valid role.
Final answer: Any two from: growth; repair of tissues by replacement of cells; replacement of old / dead / damaged cells; asexual reproduction; production of genetically identical daughter cells.

hints: Start by reading Fig. 6.2 carefully - what does the left y-axis with the dashed line show and what does the right y-axis with the solid line show as Paclitaxel concentration increases from 5 to 50 $nmol dm^{-3}$?
Describe the two opposite trends in words and pick out numbers to prove them, for example percentage at 5 and 50 $nmol dm^{-3}$ and ratio at 5 and 50.
Think about what a falling anaphase to metaphase ratio means - are cells getting stuck before they can separate their chromatids?
Link that stuck stage to the normal machinery of metaphase to anaphase, such as spindle fibres shortening and centromeres dividing.
walkthrough:
Describe Both Curves With Data**
The dashed line shows percentage of cells in stages of mitosis rises with drug concentration, from about 5% at 5 $nmol dm^{-3}$ to about 18% at 20 $nmol dm^{-3}$ to about 38% at 50 $nmol dm^{-3}$. The solid line shows the opposite: the ratio of anaphase cells to metaphase cells falls, from about 0.25 at 5 $nmol dm^{-3}$ to about 0.14 at 20 $nmol dm^{-3}$ to about 0.07 at 50 $nmol dm^{-3}$.

Interpret What the Ratio Fall Means**
A lower anaphase to metaphase ratio means a greater proportion of mitotic cells are in metaphase than in anaphase. In other words, as concentration increases, more cells stop in metaphase or spend more time there, and fewer are able to move into anaphase. That also explains why the total percentage in mitosis builds up - cells enter mitosis but cannot finish it.

Suggest a Mechanism for Metaphase Arrest**
Normally at the end of metaphase, centromeres divide, spindle fibres shorten and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles. Paclitaxel appears to block this step, for example by preventing spindle fibre shortening so chromatids stay together and cells cannot pass the metaphase checkpoint. This halts uncontrolled mitosis, which is useful against cancer.

Final answer: As [Paclitaxel] increases from 5 to 50 $nmol dm^{-3}$: percentage of cells in mitosis increases from approx. 5% to approx. 38%; ratio of cells in anaphase to cells in metaphase decreases from approx. 0.25 to approx. 0.07. More cells accumulate / spend longer in metaphase and fewer progress to anaphase, suggesting Paclitaxel prevents spindle fibres shortening / centromeres dividing / sister chromatids moving to opposite poles, so cells do not pass the metaphase checkpoint.
